Taiwan is likely to be overshadowed as presidents Xi Jinping and Donald Trump are expected to meet on the sidelines of the Asia Pacific Economic Forum this week, even as the threat from China evolves and grows stronger.
Leaders from China, the U.S. and some 21 other economies will gather at the APEC summit this week in Shenzhen, China. Recent events like the scandal that forced Nvidia's CEO to resign, export controls and the ongoing trade dispute have made the tech competition between Beijing and Washington all the more pressing.
Few expect major breakthroughs on Taiwan, a self-ruled island that is claimed by Beijing. While the U.S. does not formally recognize Taiwan, it is the island’s biggest informal ally and seller of arms.
“For the Trump administration, this isn’t a core issue between the U.S. and China,” said Arthur Zhin-Sheng Wang, an expert on cross-Straits relations at Taiwan’s Central Police University.
US-Taiwan ties remain strong behind the scenes
Experts largely say that cooperation with the U.S. remains strong below the level of rhetoric, despite Trump’s public ambivalence toward Taiwan.
One sign of this came from the summer, when the de facto United States embassy in Taiwan posted a photo showing joint patrols between the two coast guards, a rare occurrence, as the U.S. does not usually acknowledge it has direct cooperation with Taiwan in any defense capacity.
“This also is proof of the decades that Taiwan and U.S. have had of cooperation and training. I was also surprised,” said Kuo Yu-jen, a defense studies expert and director of the Institute for National Policy Research in Taiwan.
The U.S. is obligated by law to help Taiwan defend itself, which has manifested in the form of arms sales, while the government officially adopts a stance of ambiguity on whether it would intervene militarily in the case of a Chinese invasion.
The Taiwanese public is used to the continued uncertainties of the island’s relationship with the U.S. Research from the Institute of National Defense and Security Research in Taiwan, a government-funded think tank, showed that public attitudes toward the U.S. remain around the same. Polls conducted in the past five years show that about half of the public believes the U.S. will send soldiers to support Taiwan in the event of a Chinese invasion, and about half don’t.
“I do think they will take some actions, though it may not be sending soldiers,” said Allen Hsieh, a 28-year-old media professional in Taipei. “I think Taiwan’s importance to the U.S. is even more important than Ukraine.”
Stalled arms sales for now
Since starting his second term, Trump called for Taiwan to spend more on its own defense and Taiwan responded that it would commit to 5% of its GDP on defense.
Arms sales are ongoing. While much media attention has focused on a $14 billion package that remains stalled, an earlier package of $11 billion approved at the end of last year is in progress. Some of the stalled arms packages have been delayed since before Trump came into office, experts have also said.
Those include fighter jets. Taiwan received the first two of long-delayed F-16V fighter jets from the U.S. in October, and three more jets earlier this month. The aircraft are a part of a long list of backlogged U.S. orders worth almost $30 billion, according to the Taiwan Security Monitor research project which tracks defense-related developments on the island at George Mason University.
But the delays are not necessarily because of political considerations with China, a concern that was raised when Trump said he discussed arms sales with Xi earlier this year. Instead, it may be more of an issue with manufacturing capacity, particularly for future sales.
Congress approved the sale of long-range precision strike systems to Taiwan in December 2025, but Taiwan faces competition because of limited supplies. Kuo noted that among the missiles approved for sale are the same ones being used by the U.S. military in the ongoing Iran war, such as the HIMARS rockets and supplies were low.
“I don’t think this is a political issue. They just can’t produce so many of these missiles in a short period,” he said.
China expands coast guard role in pressure on Taiwan
Meanwhile, China has intensified its military and nonmilitary pressure on Taiwan. In 2025, the People’s Liberation Army flew about 5,448 fighter jet sorties toward the island during military exercises, according to Skyfaring, an open-source website that compiles public data from Taiwan’s Ministry of Defense. That marked a sharp increase from the years before 2023, when such flights were sporadic.
Beijing also recently held unannounced military drills in the Western Pacific, deploying more than 100 vessels in waters near Taiwan and Japan, Taiwan’s National Security Council chief Joseph Wu said in a Nov. 3 post on X.
The number of PLA flights recorded this year stood at 2,401 as of Nov. 12, below the full-year total for 2025.
“I think the threat is transforming ... for example, more of its exercises are now about blockading and sealing off” Taiwan, Wang said, rather than firing live missiles. He said Beijing was expanding its gray-zone tactics — aggressive actions that fall short of open warfare.
These include greater use of the coast guard to assert China’s claims, mirroring its approach elsewhere. In June, the Chinese coast guard began patrolling off Taiwan’s east coast, which faces the open Pacific, extending its activities beyond Taiwan’s outlying islands closer to China.
Wang compared the approach to Beijing’s tactics in the South China Sea, where Chinese coast guard vessels patrol waters disputed with the Philippines. China has also designated a shoal claimed by the Philippines as a nature reserve under Chinese protection.
“It’s telling the whole world it has sovereignty here.”

articles.title_orig: Trump Administration Tightens AI Chip Export Restrictions Ahead of China Visit
articles.title_zh: Trump Administration Tightens AI Chip Export Restrictions Ahead of China Visit
articles.content_orig:
Sen. Maria Cantwell , the top Democrat on the Senate commerce committee, alleged in a letter to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on Sunday that the department under his leadership failed to prevent China from accessing the U.S.'s most advanced artificial intelligence chips.
In the letter, Cantwell prodded Lutnick to enforce export controls and stop the flow of AI chips to companies barred from receiving the technology. She sent the missive ahead of a planned meeting this week between U.S. officials and Chinese President Xi Jinping on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation, in China.
Her urging comes as Washington reels from revelations that former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang had a relationship with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang. Nvidia is the leading U.S. company designing advanced AI chips.
Alice Huang was an executive at Singaporean technology company Megaspeed that allegedly smuggled restricted chips to China.
Lutnick, meanwhile, has come under fire for stalling efforts to crack down on chip sales to China and for his close personal relationship with Jensen Huang, who was a vocal opponent of export controls.
"The Department of Commerce has resisted efforts to restrict companies flagged as national security threats, weakened safeguards, and left open pathways for the PRC to train advanced AI models using sensitive American technology," Cantwell wrote to Lutnick. "These failures to carry out the law help give away America's technology advantage in AI."
The Commerce Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Monday.
Cantwell called on Lutnick to use his authority to enforce a 2018 law, known as the Export Control Reform Act , which gives the Commerce Department broad latitude to enforce export controls and protect sensitive American technology.
She also cites potential financial conflicts involving Lutnick's sons , who control Cantor Fitzgerald, which she said held $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock at the time of his nomination. And she notes the Trump administration's 25% fee on certain Nvidia chips sold to China, which she said could create "a perverse financial incentive to approve exports of sensitive American technology."
"America's national security and AI leadership cannot be compromised by family business interests or a policy that generates federal revenue from exporting technology critical to our competitive edge," Cantwell wrote.
Both Democratic and Republican members of Congress have ramped up pressure on Lutnick and other Commerce Department officials after a Nov. 9 New York Times report alleging the department may have slow-walked an investigation into Megaspeed.
On Thursday, Senate banking committee Chair Tim Scott , R-S.C., summoned both Huang and Lutnick t o testify before his committee in December.
Lutnick has agreed to appear before the panel, Kristen Eichamer, a Commerce Department spokesperson, said in a statement last week.
And Democrats, who will take control of both the House and Senate in January, have signaled they will investigate Jensen Huang and Commerce officials.
On Wednesday, Sen. Elizabeth Warren , D-Mass., the top Democrat on the Senate banking panel, and Sen. Chris Coons , D-Del., the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations subpanel with jurisdiction over East Asia and the Pacific, sent a letter to Lutnick, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and White House Chief of Staff Stephen Miller instructing them to preserve all documents and communications related to Nvidia's exports of "advanced AI chips to China or to entities that may divert such chips to China."
The letter gives all three officials until Nov. 17 to confirm that preservation directives have been issued.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
articles.title_zh: Trump administration moves to block China from indirect access to American AI technology
articles.content_orig:
The Commerce Department on Monday tightened export restrictions designed to prevent China from accessing sensitive, AI-powering computer chips amid a dispute in the Trump administration over how to handle the issue.
The much-anticipated Commerce rule puts new curbs on US exports to data centers that provide “significant volumes” of computing to companies based in countries subject to US arms embargoes such as China, Iran and Russia.
The move comes as President Donald Trump prepares to meet with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week, and on the heels of a scandal involving the chipmaking giant Nvidia, and its now-former CEO Jensen Huang, who has pushed for the ability to sell Nvidia chips abroad.
Huang resigned last week following revelations of extramarital affairs — including one he had with a Chinese woman who worked at Megaspeed, a Singapore-based data center company. The Commerce and Justice Departments began investigating Megaspeed, a major purchaser of Nvidia chips, in 2024 as part of a broader probe into an ecosystem of foreign companies suspected of diverting Nvidia chips to China, CNN has reported .
The Nvidia saga has put greater public scrutiny on the Commerce Department’s role in regulating the sale of crucial American technologies abroad. Earlier this month, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent challenged Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick in a Situation Room meeting over his department’s reluctance to label Nvidia customer Megaspeed a possible national security threat.
The new rule is also a replacement for a Joe Biden-era export control rule that the Trump administration let lapse last year. Trump officials saw the Biden policy as an impediment to American businesses.
The Commerce Department had resisted putting the new rule into place for some time while other top officials in the Trump administration had been pushing for it, including Bessent, Secretary of State Marco Rubio and US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, sources said.
That dynamic could be significant going forward because Commerce holds the tools of enforcement. Experts noted that the rule itself appeared to be strong but that the implementation would determine whether or not it has teeth.
The rule is “the first good-faith effort to actually close loopholes in export controls in a year and a half,” said Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations.
With the Commerce Department announcement coming the same week that Trump is set to travel to China, administration officials are also bracing for a Chinese response, according to a senior administration official. But some expect that any response will come after Trump’s visit largely because China wants to avoid dramatic tension during the meeting, the official said.
At a press briefing on Tuesday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing “will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
Spokesperson Guo Jiakun said the new restrictions were “a typical case of economic coercion and long-arm jurisdiction. It runs counter to the consensus reached by both sides.”
The Commerce Department noted that the rule was “written by and at the direction of the Department of Treasury and the National Security Council.”
But as Trump left the White House on Monday on his way to Asia, he downplayed reported disagreements inside his administration on the matter and said he has no plans to fire Lutnick, who some officials have argued should have done more to limit the sale of advanced chips to China.
Trump acknowledged that Bessent and Lutnick “have two different views” on how fast Commerce should have acted.
“They’re fine,” Trump said of the two Cabinet secretaries. “One wants to be friendly with China, and one wants to have a blow up with China.”
For his part, Trump defended the decision to delay labeling Megaspeed a national security threat.
“Well, he might have delayed it, but he was doing that because you could have, if you didn’t delay it, if you did do something, you could have a blow-up with China,” Trump told CNN’s Alayna Treene.
“We’re having a very good relationship with China right now, and I understand both sides of it. And I’ll make a decision, but I understand very well both sides,” he added.
Trump also on Monday offered a vote of confidence to Huang, saying he “would not mind” if the former Nvidia CEO were reinstated atop the chipmaking firm.
“I would not mind that,” Trump told reporters. “I think he learned a big lesson, I guess maybe one lesson more important than the other. But I would certainly not mind seeing that.”
The president’s support came amid reports that Huang was discussing the possibility of a comeback effort just days after resigning under pressure over revelations of extramarital affairs — including one with a woman suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence. (A source familiar said Nvidia’s board is not considering bringing Huang back.)
Trump — who called Huang a “legend” in the hours after he stepped down — has repeatedly praised him despite the longstanding national security concerns about Huang harbored by some senior officials in his administration.
This story has been updated with additional information.
Hadas Gold contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: Critical bridges in Crimea and Kyiv damaged as Russia and Ukraine exchange large-scale attacks
articles.title_zh: Critical bridges in Crimea and Kyiv damaged as Russia and Ukraine exchange large-scale attacks
articles.content_orig:
A section of a multi-billion dollar strategic bridge connecting Russia and the occupied Crimean Peninsula has collapsed following a Ukrainian strike. Meanwhile, much of Kyiv was brought to a standstill on Tuesday after Moscow hit two of its key bridges overnight.
The Crimean Bridge, also known as the Kerch Bridge, is a vital supply line for Moscow’s troops and has huge symbolic value for Russian President Vladimir Putin, who made its construction a key priority after Russia’s illegal annexation of the Ukrainian peninsula in 2014.
Ukraine has stepped up its attacks against Crimea in the past six months, forcing the Russian-installed authorities to impose a state of emergency over the summer because of widespread power outages and fuel shortages on the heavily militarized peninsula.
The timing of the latest attack, on the eve of Putin’s meeting with US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Asia, makes it even more symbolic.
The Kremlin has sought to frame the gathering as a “New Yalta” in a nod to the 1945 conference at which the Soviet leader Joseph Stalin effectively redrew the global map of spheres of influence with the Allied powers. The attack on the bridge makes Yalta, a city in annexed Crimea, effectively inaccessible from mainland Russia, at least until it is repaired.
The $3.7 billion bridge, which at nearly 12 miles is the longest crossing in Europe, was built to handle 40,000 cars a day and move 14 million passengers and 13 million tons of cargo per year, according to Russian state media.
Videos and images geolocated by CNN appear to show a portion of the road bridge collapsed into the water. The parallel rail bridge appeared still to be standing. In another video geolocated by CNN, a fire can be seen burning on a section of the bridge.
US floated idea of Ukraine swapping land for NATO membership, Zelensky says
Traffic has been suspended following the second Ukrainian attack in as many days, Russia’s transport ministry said, adding that the bridge was damaged in a drone attack.
“Experts are assessing the damage,” said the ministry, adding that there were no casualties.
Russia’s Investigative Committee confirmed the attack on the bridge, calling it a “terrorist act by Ukrainian armed groups.”
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted the Kerch Bridge since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, but the damage the bridge sustained this week appears to be more significant than in some of the previous attacks.
Russia’s military said its air defenses had shot down 1,441 Ukrainian drones overnight.
The Ukrainian capital Kyiv also came under intense bombardment overnight into Tuesday. Two people were killed and the city’s North and South bridges badly damaged in the assault, officials said.
Kyiv is split in half by the Dnipro River. The right bank is home to the majority of the city’s business centers, offices and government institutions, while the left bank is mostly residential.
The bridges connecting the two sides are crucial – some 600,000 vehicles as well as trains and Kyiv’s metro cross them every day.
“Critical infrastructure systems have been damaged, causing disruptions to water and heat supply in some districts,” the city office said.
The attacks on the bridges have led to major traffic jams on both the left and right banks, although the scale of damage was still being clarified, officials said.
Russia’s military said it had targeted Ukrainian military, transportation, energy and port infrastructure, using drones and ground- and air-based precision-guided weapons.
The exchange of attacks on critical infrastructure come two days before the planned trilateral talks between Trump, Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, China on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ summit.
Trump said Monday he expects to discuss the war in Ukraine with his Russian and Chinese counterparts, despite US officials suggesting last week the topic wouldn’t be on the table.
How Trump is hoping to use an Asia trip to reassert his authority
“We’ll talk about my favorite subject, Ukraine,” Trump told reporters as he departed the White House.
“Ukraine’s losing – Ukraine-Russia is losing 25,000 soldiers a month, so we’ll be talking about that,” he said, without giving any source for that claim. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte said last week that Russia was losing “more than 40,000 troops – killed or seriously wounded – every month.”
In October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky voiced concern that a trilateral meeting between Trump, Xi and Putin might lead to dealmaking about the future of Ukraine without consulting Kyiv.
CNN’s Kevin Liptak and Daria Tarasova-Markina contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, CNBC reports
articles.title_zh: Nvidia warns chip buyers of legal risks tied to China AI access, CNBC reports
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia warned its customers that new legislation on Chinese companies remotely accessing its artificial-intelligence chips could expose it and them to U.S. "legal action," sources told CNBC.
The chip giant is facing increasing scrutiny from U.S. lawmakers over Chinese companies' access to its advanced chips, which U.S. export controls restrict from going to China.
Nvidia messaged chip buyers in recent months to caution that the proposed Remote Access Security Act, or RASA, would give the U.S. government broader authority to control access to cloud services in the same way as physical hardware, potentially exposing both parties to legal risk, according to two people with direct knowledge of the matter. The people asked not to be named while discussing private communications.
It also said that, for now, it would not sell its chips to customers who rent more than 50% of the graphics processing units, or GPUs, to Chinese companies, the people said.
Separately, the Financial Times reported earlier this month that Nvidia verbally told data-center clients to direct at least 51% of their services to non-Chinese customers under future contracts.
Regulators have had limited powers to control companies' access to those chips through cloud services hosted overseas.
RASA passed the House of Representatives in January but has not yet passed the Senate. Remote access to the chips has provoked the ire of President Donald Trump 's administration, which has sought to keep the chips out of China to maintain the U.S. lead in the AI race.
CNBC reported on Nov. 5 that Chinese lab Moonshot AI sought access to Nvidia chips through data centers in Europe. The Trump administration previously singled the company out, accusing it in July of accessing the chips through centers in East Asia.
The U.S. Commerce Department's Bureau of Industry and Security, or BIS, announced on Monday an interim final rule designed to prevent Chinese companies' remote access to AI chips.
Nvidia and BIS did not respond to a request for comment.
On Sunday, U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called for a "dramatic shakeup" at Nvidia after Jensen Huang 's shock departure as CEO, amid reports of an extramarital affair with a woman U.S. authorities reportedly suspect of spying for China.
Bessent suggested other Nvidia executives should face scrutiny over the chip giant's compliance with export controls.
"I want to keep coming back to what was the culture at Nvidia, and were they pressing these seemingly illicit sales to goose their revenues and their earnings?" Bessent told Fox News.
In an August securities filing , Nvidia said it sought to "strictly comply with all applicable export control regulators" but did not have "physical control of our products after sale" and relied on its customers' and partners' compliance programs.
Huang has been asked to testify before the Senate Banking Committee on Dec. 3.

articles.content_orig:
Akira Kurabayashi, a company director and head of the software development division at ARIKA , passed away suddenly on November 14, 2026, due to heart failure, ARIKA president Akira Nishitani announced .
Kurabayashi previously worked as a game programmer at TAITO , where he served as main programmer on titles such as Darius Gaiden , Fighters’ Impact , and Vertexer . After joining ARIKA, he served as both a company director and the head of the software development division, contributing to numerous titles through major industry transitions like 2D to 3D, arcade to home consoles, and the introduction of online multiplayer.
A memorial service is being planned in accordance with his family’s wishes.

articles.title_orig: Trump is to arrive in the Philippines to talk trade and seek respite from troubles at home
articles.title_zh: Trump is to arrive in the Philippines to talk trade and seek respite from troubles at home
articles.content_orig:
The president heads to China tomorrow, where he’ll join historic talks with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin.
• Trump in Asia: President Donald Trump has landed to pomp and ceremony in the Philippines for the first stop of an Asia trip set to be dominated by questions about AI and the US relationship with China. The Philippines has seen protests ahead of his arrival over US-led plans to build data centers in the country.
• Historic trilateral: His trip includes an unprecedented meeting with the authoritarian leaders of China and Russia , where Trump said he will discuss the war in Ukraine . Trump also said he “may meet” with Kim Jong Un , should the North Korean leader also make an appearance in China this week.
• Semiconductor scandal looms: Trump said he “might” discuss Nvidia founder Jensen Huang’s reported affair with an alleged Chinese intelligence asset in his separate one-on-one meeting with Xi.
President Donald Trump has landed in Manila for the first stop of an Asia trip that will be dominated by questions about AI technology and the US relationship with China.
Trump landed at Ninoy Aquino International Airport after a nearly 18-hour journey from Washington, including a refueling stop in Alaska.
You can watch this at the top of this page by scrolling up and pressing play.
He’ll be greeted at the airport by the US ambassador to the Philippines, Lee Lipton, along with a delegation of Filipino officials – including Ferdinand Alexander Marcos III, the House Majority Leader in the Philippines who is the son of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. (and the grandson of the longtime strongman leader Ferdinand Marcos Sr.).
President Donald Trump will arrive in the Philippines to protests against data centers planned in the country as part of a US-led plan to dominate AI.
The Philippines is one of 26 signatories of Pax Silica, a US State Department-led initiative to lure AI-related industries away from Chinese supply chains.
But there is growing anger in the country over plans to build a 1,620 hectare technology hub near a former American military base in Luzon as part of the project.
The hub will be built in Capas, Tarlac, which was the endpoint of the “death march” of Filipino and American prisoners of war during World War II. It is also home to indigenous peoples called the Aeta, who traveled to the capital Manila to protest possibly being displaced from their ancestral lands.
Protesters opposing the knock-on economic impacts from the US-Iran war and the US-led Pax Silica initiative clashed with police in the Philippines ahead of the ASEAN summit on Sunday. More than 200 people were arrested, according to police.
Protesters clashed with police in the Philippines ahead of the ASEAN summit, opposing the US-Iran war’s economic impact and the US-led Pax Silica initiative. CNN’s Will Ripley reports from Manila.
Backers say the initiative would inject billions of dollars in foreign investment. Indigenous communities , environmental activists and farmer groups are concerned about power usage, water consumption and land rights.
The US remains a top export market, investor and foremost defense ally of Manila. But tariffs, and the spike in energy prices sparked by Washington’s war with Iran have exposed the risks of heavy reliance on Washington.
An open divide among President Donald Trump’s advisers over China has burst into public view this week. That could make for an awkward flight aboard Air Force One, where many of the warring advisers have been sequestered now for hours.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are all accompanying Trump as he makes the nearly 20-hour journey from Washington to Manila.
Bessent recently publicly heaped blame on Lutnick’s department for slow-walking new restrictions on AI technology going to China, claiming the rest of the president’s advisers all favored tighter rules.
It underscored an internal debate that has been roiling the administration for months. The scandal involving Nvidia and its former CEO Jensen Huang has thrust the issue into the foreground.
Trump appeared to defend Lutnick as he was departing the White House, saying he was looking to avoid confrontation with Beijing.
American officials now say they just aren’t sure how Trump plans to handle the Nvidia matter in his meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping this week, leading to a measure of anxiety over what he’ll say in the meeting.
US officials said last week the spying allegations against Alice Huang, the former Megaspeed executive suspected of having ties to Chinese intelligence, wouldn’t be up for discussion at all.
But Trump has downplayed the national security concerns, and appeared not to remember having been briefed on the topic by Rubio during another trip to China this year.
He would not rule out bringing the issue up with Xi . Some administration officials are worried he could take a conciliatory tone in the hopes of maintaining a good relationship.
At their last meeting, President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping seemed ready to back away from confrontation amid an escalating tech rivalry, and even potentially collaborate on AI development safeguards.
The Nvidia scandal could end all that.
Days before Trump is set to meet Xi in Shenzhen, the US Commerce Department increased restrictions on exports of advanced US semiconductors in an effort to further limit China’s access to them.
The measures announced Monday will apply to overseas data centers that supply “significant volumes” of computing power to a list of countries including China, and require new licenses for exports to Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, Thailand or Brazil, due to a “higher-than-normal risk” of diversion, or rerouting chips to unauthorized buyers.
The rule change follows growing controversy over Nvidia, the world’s biggest supplier of advanced AI chips, and its sales to a Singapore-based company Megaspeed that is under investigation for potentially diverting server shipments to China.
Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned last week after reports he had an affair with Megaspeed executive Alice Huang, whom US officials suspected of being part of an intelligence operation by China.
Beijing has called the allegations groundless and an attempt to smear China. But the scandal has bolstered US efforts to strengthen tech export controls, which could derail recent efforts to ease trade tensions or even provoke retaliation from China.
At a press briefing on Tuesday, a Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson said Beijing “will take necessary measures to resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
Read more about the tightened restrictions here.
US President Donald Trump said he “may meet” with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un during his visit to China, adding that it would be up to Beijing’s leader Xi Jinping.
Trump is traveling to Shenzhen, China later this week to attend the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, where he plans to hold trilateral talks with Xi and Russian President Vladimir Putin.
Trump has repeatedly said he wishes to meet with the North Korean leader. North Korea is not a member of APEC and Kim has not confirmed any plans to attend the summit. At a news briefing Tuesday, Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun said he had no information on whether Kim would attend APEC this week.
Kim’s travel habits could make an impromptu meeting difficult. The leader is known to travel on a heavily armored train that reportedly travels at an average speed of 37 miles per hour. Shenzhen is more than 1,000 miles from the North Korean border.
Kim took a 2.5 day train journey across China to meet Trump in Hanoi, Vietnam in 2019.

articles.title_orig: Trump Backs Huang Comeback While Nvidia Board Seeks New CEO
articles.title_zh: Trump Backs Huang Comeback While Nvidia Board Seeks New CEO
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Something pretty remarkable is happening in Silicon Valley right now. One shouldn't be surprised, considering the profit motives of many invested in the AI ecosystem and that what Nvidia ( NVDA ) does lies at the center of it all.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned as the company's CEO under a cloud of controversy he created, and suddenly some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley are organizing a campaign to bring him back.
Nvidia stock slipped 0.3% before the bell on Tuesday.
Tesla ( TSLA ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) CEO Elon Musk has signed on to the "Bring Jensen Back" petition. Other prominent executives have joined, including Uber ( UBER ) founder Travis Kalanick — who left Uber unceremoniously after his own string of highly publicized missteps.
Read more: Live updates on Nvidia ahead of the AI chip titan's earnings
The online petition has attracted more than 180,000 signatures. Nvidia employees have also taken to X and LinkedIn to voice their support for Huang.
Let's be clear: Jensen Huang is an extraordinary entrepreneur . A once-in-a-lifetime type of talent. He helped build Nvidia into one of the world's most important companies, with a market cap that neared $5 trillion earlier this year. His impact on the AI revolution is enormous and will not be forgotten.
But here's the issue a lot of people are right to point out: Being a brilliant CEO does not make you untouchable.
Huang admitted to being unfaithful to Lori, his wife of more than 40 years. There are serious questions surrounding his relationship with a reported Chinese spy. Additional reports say Jensen had affairs with two Nvidia employees, one of whom, Kimberly Powell , was a direct report.
All of these allegations and the broader circumstances deserve a thorough, independent investigation by the board and the law firm leading it, Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz. They should not be treated as proven facts.
And that's precisely the point.
This isn't just about one man's personal life. It's about corporate governance, national security, the responsibilities of a CEO, and the standards expected of someone running one of America's most strategically important companies.
Nvidia's board has a responsibility to shareholders, employees, and the country — not to Silicon Valley's celebrity CEO culture.
Jensen Huang absolutely deserves due process. But he is not bigger than Nvidia. And no CEO, no matter how brilliant, should be.

articles.title_orig: Leaked Files Show Deutsche Bank Protected Russian Profits Despite Warnings
articles.title_zh: Leaked Files Show Deutsche Bank Protected Russian Profits Despite Warnings
articles.content_orig:
Deutsche Bank’s headquarters in Frankfurt. The bank long resisted breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under President Vladimir V. Putin. Credit... Felix Schmitt for The New York Times
By Russ Buettner Khadija Sharife Brian Fitzpatrick Frederik Obermaier Bastian Obermayer and Sophia Baumann
When Russian missiles began pummeling Ukraine in February 2022, executives at one of the world’s largest banks sensed trouble headed their way.
Within hours of an invasion that set off a war that is now in its fifth year, Western governments issued new financial sanctions intended to further isolate Russia from the world economy.
At Deutsche Bank, a longtime bank of Russian industry titans and oligarchs, officials scrambled to get ahead of the damage. “Russian Sanctions Urgent Request” read the subject line of an email sent by one of Deutsche’s anti-financial crime specialists to her colleagues.
“As you know we have a large Russian Oligarchs client population” and other clients with investments in Russian companies, she wrote. She asked which of those clients “we potentially could unwind and which not.” Should the bank advise them, she wondered, to withdraw their money “while they still can?”
This email exchange was the beginning of a frenzied reckoning within the scandal-plagued bank over its long resistance to breaking with Russia’s most important business titans under Vladimir V. Putin, the Russian president. The bank’s clients included the Russian billionaires Oleg V. Deripaska and Viktor F. Vekselberg. Time and again over many years, records show, Deutsche Bank’s risk managers warned that such relationships were perilous.
But profits associated with maintaining its Russian clients won out every time.
Russia’s war in Ukraine swept up Deutsche Bank in a larger shift. For decades, German politicians and business leaders believed that working with Russia and deepening economic ties between the two countries would discourage Russian aggression. That strategy collapsed after the invasion.

articles.title_orig: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.title_zh: Facing Criticism, Trump Administration Says It’s Investigating Megaspeed
articles.content_orig:
The Justice and Commerce Departments announced late Monday that they were pursuing a criminal investigation of Megaspeed, a Singapore company once led by a woman whom U.S. officials believe worked as a Chinese intelligence asset while having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive.
The announcement appeared to be an effort to counter criticism that Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick was slow to investigate Megaspeed. It has become the most prominent example of companies that American authorities believe are skirting export rules on the powerful artificial intelligence chips made by Nvidia, the world’s leading manufacturer.
Nvidia exports have exposed a rift in the Trump administration between officials who believe American A.I. technology needs to be kept out of China for national security reasons and others who want a more hands-off approach to export controls.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said in a TV interview on Friday that his department had been pushing for months to add Megaspeed to a trade blacklist, but that the Commerce Department “holds the pen.”
“You will have to ask them about their internal processes,” he said.
That the Justice Department was included in the Monday night announcement appeared to add heft to the investigation’s importance and signaled to critics that administration officials did not intend to ignore the issue.
Megaspeed was created and led for a time by Alice Huang, who U.S. officials say was an asset for Chinese intelligence. The New York Times reported last year that she and Nvidia’s chief executive, Jensen Huang, had a close relationship, and last week Mr. Huang admitted that he had been unfaithful to his wife with Ms. Huang.

articles.title_orig: Papua New Guinea prime minister tells Xi it 'wasn't easy' to close Taiwan office
articles.title_zh: Papua New Guinea prime minister tells Xi it 'wasn't easy' to close Taiwan office
articles.content_orig:
Taipei, Nov. 12 (CNA) Taiwan foreign ministry officials said Thursday that China was behind Papua New Guinea's (PNG) sudden decision last week to expel Taiwanese diplomats and demand the closure of the Taiwan representative office there.
PNG Foreign Minister Justin Tkatchenko first made the demand on July 16 for the closure of the Taiwan representative office, citing his country's adherence to the "one-China" policy, said Lin Hung-hsun (林宏勳), deputy director-general of the foreign ministry's Department of East Asian and Pacific Affairs.
Taiwan and PNG subsequently engaged in talks over the matter, and it was agreed that PNG would give Taiwan one year's written notice to close the representative office, Lin said during a legislative hearing.
However, on Nov. 6, PNG raised the issue again, demanding that Taiwanese diplomats there leave the country within seven days, he said.
Also answering questions at the legislative hearing, Deputy Foreign Minister Chen Ming-chi (陳明祺) said he believed PNG's about-turn was driven by pressure from China.
He pointed out that a high-level PNG delegation had visited China just last week, while PNG Prime Minister James Marape is scheduled to travel to China next week to attend the APEC summit.
"Given these circumstances, our assessment is that the government of Papua New Guinea may have been subjected to significant pressure from China or even offered economic incentives," Chen said.
For instance, China has announced that it stands ready to increase its imports of liquefied natural gas (LNG) from PNG, following Taiwan's decision to stop purchasing LNG from the Pacific nation after PNG demanded the closure of the Taiwan representative office there, Chen said.
Chen and Lin were answering lawmakers' questions about the closure of the Taiwan Economic Office, as it was named, which was first opened in 1990 in Port Moresby, PNG.
On Nov. 6, PNG's Department of Foreign Affairs said its secretary, Elias Wohengu, had given notice to the head of the Taiwan Economic Office Chiu Chen-yu (邱陳煜) to leave the country within seven days.
The seven-day notice also applied to the office's First Secretary Lee Chung-nun, while the one remaining diplomat, Pan Shao-jyun, would be allowed to stay to oversee the office's closure within a year, the department said in a statement.
The department also said that on Oct. 6, it had given Taiwan 12 months' notice to complete the closure of the office.
"It should not be interpreted as an assurance that all existing staffing and operational arrangements will remain unchanged throughout that period," the department said.
In response, Taiwan's Ministry of Foreign Affairs (MOFA) announced the same day that it would close the office and withdraw all personnel stationed there.
MOFA also said it would conduct a comprehensive review and adjustment of Taiwan's ties with PNG, "in consideration of national dignity, diplomatic autonomy, and overall national interests."
Since then, Taiwan has been withdrawing its diplomatic and technical mission personnel from PNG, according to MOFA.
PNG is a diplomatic ally of China, which does not permit its allies to maintain simultaneous diplomatic relations with Taiwan.

articles.title_orig: They’re Young, Frustrated and Want France to Change. They Disagree on How.
articles.title_zh: They’re Young, Frustrated and Want France to Change. They Disagree on How.
articles.content_orig:
Soumaya Sarré, 18, is a history and Arabic studies undergraduate who grew up in a working-class district on the edge of Paris. She is a voice of the youth-led protests that have spurred unrest across France since September. “I can carry our voices, the voices of young people from working-class neighborhoods,” she told me.
Louise Montangon, 22, is a philosophy undergraduate from rural France. As the student protests gained momentum, she became one of their leading critics, regularly condemning the young demonstrators on television panels and social media. “The majority of university and high school students actually want to attend their classes,” she said in an interview.
Unknown to the public until this fall, these two women from opposite ends of the political spectrum have surfaced as emblems of the combustible French moment, which was set to intensify again on Tuesday with more strikes and protests.
Ms. Sarré and Ms. Montangon aren’t formal leaders of their political camps, and their sudden prominence partly reflects society’s tendency to search for avatars for leaderless movements. Their simultaneous rise, and their divergent politics, nevertheless reflect the polarization of French society, and particularly its youth — five months from a presidential election dominated by candidates from the far-left and the far-right.
Polls of people under 25 suggest that more than 40 percent support the main far-left candidate, Jean-Luc Mélenchon, while more than 20 percent back his far-right opponent, Marine Le Pen. In legislative elections in 2024, nearly half of voters from that age group voted for Mr. Mélenchon’s party, and a third voted for Ms. Le Pen’s.
Support for moderate solutions has plummeted after years of centrist governance under Emmanuel Macron, France’s term-limited president.

articles.title_zh: Taiwan may take a backseat when Xi and Trump meet for a third time at an APEC summit
articles.content_orig:
Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged in Please refresh your browser to be logged in
Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.
US president Donald Trump heads to Asia this week to take part in back-to-back summits on economic cooperation, world conflicts, and nuclear weapons.
Much of the world’s focus will be on the historic, first-ever trilateral meeting between Trump, Russian leader Vladimir Putin and China’s Xi Jinping on Thursday.
However, hours before leaving the White House for the Philippines, Trump managed to raise the stakes even further while suggesting North Korean leader could also join them.
“(Xi) was here a month ago, and we're also going to meet with (Russian) President Putin, and we may meet with Kim Jong Un also,” Trump said.
“So that'll be good. We have a chance to accomplish a lot.,” while stressing the decision on Kim’s attendance was up to Beijing.
Despite the strategic importance of the issues on the agenda during the trip, it could still be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal.
CEO Jensen Huang was forced to resign last week after it emerged he had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy. The ousted tech boss has close ties to the US president, even accompanying him on Air Force One during his last trip to China in May.
However Trump is not expected to directly raise the spy allegations with Xi, one senior US administration told Reuters on condition of anonymity.
The US president is due tol land in Manila on Tuesday for the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit, before flying to Shenzhen in southern China late on Wednesday for the two-day Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) forum, at the end of which the first-ever three-way discussion between Xi, Trump, and ‌Putin will take place.
“The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” said a White House spokesperson.
A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February. It is the first time since the early 1970s that there is no legally binding limits on US and Russian nuclear forces without another agreement being under negotiation.
Russia and the US possess the largest nuclear arsenal in the world, followed by China.
The United Nations has long urged for nuclear disarmament, warning that rising geopolitical tensions have fuelled nuclear risks around the world.
“If there is a denuclearisation program, we are ready to be fully engaged in that and contribute to make it a success,” UN ​Secretary-General Antonio ‌Guterres said on Monday in Manila, where he is attending the Asean summit.
The denuclearisation talks will also spotlight the war in Iran, with Tehran being a strategic partner of both China and Russia.
Leaders at Asean are likely to renew calls for peaceful resolutions of conflicts, including in the South China Sea and in Myanmar. They are expected to push for efforts to protect their economies and citizens from the continuing fallout from global conflicts, such as the blockade of the Strait of Hormuz in the Persian Gulf.
The White House has said that Trump plans to sign a trade deal with Thailand while in Manila, while US officials will also meet on the sidelines with the so-called Quad, or Quadrilateral Security Dialogue, which consists of Australia, India, Japan and the US.
Trump will be looking for an overseas success on the trip, following the disastrous midterm results that saw his Republican party lose control of Congress.
“The president will undoubtedly be seeking to use this trip to reassert leadership, authority, demonstrate his statesmanship capabilities and essentially show off on the international stage,” Kurt Tong, a former US ambassador for Apec, told Bloomberg.
The US president will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday.
But expectations for progress at the talks in China are not high. No agreement is expected afterward, a senior US official said, according to AP and Reuters.
“In China, the administration has been trying to lower expectations; there will be no substantive progress made between Trump and Xi,” US-based geopolitical analyst Greg Poling told PBS News .
“With Trump politically weakened after the midterm drubbing here, it is likely that the Chinese side will be even less interested in making any compromises,” he said.
Other critical issues at these summits will include AI supply chains and governance, tariff reductions and the green energy transition.

articles.title_orig: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
articles.title_zh: Two major Kyiv bridges hit in Russian attack, mayor says
articles.content_orig:
Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko at the site of a missile strike in October
Two major bridges in the Ukrainian capital have reportedly been struck in a Russian ballistic missile attack, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said.
The missiles hit Kyiv's Northern and Southern bridges spanning the Dnipro River, Klitschko said, adding that water and power supplies had been disrupted.
Meanwhile, Ukraine struck the landmark Kerch Bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea killing two people, the region's Moscow-installed governor said.
President Volodymyr Zelensky had earlier warned that Moscow might launch further strikes on the country on Monday night, after Ukrainian, US and European officials held further talks aimed at ending the years-long conflict.
Those online talks, attended by US envoy Jared Kushner and US special envoy Steve Witkoff, came after Russia said it recorded the largest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began.
Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems".
"Some areas are experiencing disruptions to water and heating supplies", he added.
Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services have been damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.
Residents of Kyiv typically shelter in the city's underground stations during air raids.
Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv. An estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.
Several of the capital's major bridges were also targeted by Russian drone strikes in October .
Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.
Separately, the Ukrainian military struck the Kerch Bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea for a second consecutive day , the region's Moscow-installed governor Sergei Aksyonov said on Telegram.
Traffic across the bridge had been suspended, he added.
The landmark bridge, which has come under repeated attack by Ukrainian forces, was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014.
Russian President Vladimir Putin inaugurated the bridge to great fanfare in 2018. The severity of the latest strike on Kerch Bridge is still unclear, though it is protected with multiple layers of aerial and maritime defences.
Russian military intercepted and destroyed 2,049 drones and four Flamingo long-distance missiles over 24 hours, officials said. Around 600 flew towards the capital alone, Moscow Mayor Sergey Sobyanin said.
The latest round of tit-for-tat strikes came after US, Ukrainian and European officials held talks on ways to facilitate "direct engagement" between Russia and Europe to end the war.
Following Monday's meeting, US envoy Jared Kushner, President Trump's son-in-law, said the US was committed to providing Ukraine with a "strong, credible security guarantees", as well as a path towards EU membership.
He added that Nato "will remain a critical pillar of European security", and that preparations are underway for a further multilateral meeting "in the near future".
In an address on Monday evening, Zelensky said that the meeting was "difficult", adding that more needed to be done to support Ukraine's defence against Russian ballistic missile strikes.
Zelensky said that Europe was represented for the first time by the full delegation that will participate in negotiations with Moscow - including the UK, France, Germany, Italy, Poland, the EU and Nato.
The Ukrainian president has long called for European delegates to be included in any peace talks, which he argues is necessary because of Kyiv's longer-term ambition to join the European Union.
He also said that Moscow is receiving "dozens of missiles per month" from North Korea.
Meanwhile, Ukrainian officials said that the final death toll from a Russian attack on the southern Ukrainian village of Kamyshuvakha earlier this month had reached 72.
Four people are still considered missing after the bombing, which Ukrainian officials say is one of the deadliest individual attacks since the start of the war in 2022.
Footage, from a camera on one of the killed police officers, showed residents going to an underground shelter after the initial attack on 2 November. Soon after a blast is heard and flames are seen as the shelter is hit.
Ukrainian police said of those killed were police officers, "staff of the gymnasium, utility workers and medical personnel".
Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.

articles.title_orig: Trump administration's $50B air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in the Senate
articles.title_zh: Trump administration's $50B air traffic demand hits GOP turbulence in the Senate
articles.content_orig:
Airports were thrown into chaos, with hundreds of flights canceled and thousands of travelers stranded. A Federal Aviation Administration investigation soon traced the disaster to an unlikely source: A router that had locked up the nation’s air traffic control network.
That incident happened 17 years ago – leading to urgent calls for FAA upgrades.
Yet on Friday, an eerily similar scene played out, this time with a rare nationwide halt to all flights as communications with pilots broke down.
Once again, the FAA now suspects the problems began with a single router, newly installed in a remote radio outpost in Arkansas.
While federal investigators with the FBI and FAA are still working to untangle exactly what went wrong last week – and who is to blame – the similar 2009 incident is a startling illustration of how long US officials have battled to upgrade an aging flight control network.
A CNN review of government oversight reports and past incidents vividly shows how decades of warnings about the FAA’s aging infrastructure have failed to head off the kind of mass outages that again struck America’s aviation industry on Friday.
“We’ve known the system has been antiquated for many years,” said Margaret Wallace, an assistant professor of aviation management at the Florida Institute of Technology. “Much of what was there can almost date back to World War II.”
The Trump administration has touted its plans to speedily replace antiquated copper wiring with fiber optics and newer equipment and pointed to Friday’s outage as evidence that Congress needs to provide more than the $12.5 billion already earmarked for upgrades.
“Congress did give me $12.5 billion, but they were very specific on how we spend it,” Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said on Sunday . “I have no money for a new network. I don’t have any new money to build new software to separate planes in the air space.”
But Friday’s incident, which Duffy said occurred during one of those upgrades, has also sharpened questions about how effectively the administration and its key contractors are carrying out the improvements already in progress.
Similar concerns were raised in September in a US Government Accountability Office report warning the FAA could potentially cause more breakdowns by moving too hastily in efforts to modernize its systems.
The report stated the FAA had made progress in replacing thousands of old copper wires with high-speed fiber optic cables but also expressed concern that the agency had not effectively scheduled those replacements to “reduce impacts to controller operations.”
“FAA could be prioritizing speed over costs and air traffic disruptions,” stated the GAO report , which added, “If these risks are realized, FAA would need to continue to rely on severely outdated systems that are prone to failure leading to more flight delays and safety incidents.”
The infrastructure that keeps thousands of flights safely separated in US airspace is built on a network of comparatively ancient technology – from copper phone lines to old computers, all of which must link a complex nationwide network of air traffic controllers.
Government officials have long sounded alarms about breakdowns in that system, which at times has failed spectacularly.
In 2009, an FAA telecommunications outage affected more than 100 air traffic facilities and grounded hundreds of flights nationwide.
A review by the Department of Transportation’s inspector general later found a technician had “incorrectly configured” a router, which caused an improper flow of air traffic data that blocked much of the system.
The technician described in the IG’s report worked for Harris Corporation, which later merged with another business to form L3Harris, the contractor now under scrutiny for the latest outage.
An FAA review panel later recommended a spate of improvements in the wake of that mass outage, including looking into setting up new backup systems.
Eight years later, though, the FAA’s inspector general warned that technology disruptions were still a major threat to the nation’s air travel – citing a number of other recent failures, including a fire in Chicago and a flood in Texas that disabled control towers for long periods of time.
“Significant work remains to mitigate the impact of air traffic control disruptions,” the 2017 report found .
In 2023, the FAA briefly halted all domestic flight departures after another  outage. A subsequent GAO report found many air traffic control systems were increasingly prone to failures and relied on hard-to-find spare parts.
The assessment determined that more than a third of the systems were “unsustainable,” with others heading in the same direction. That same year, a safety review team explicitly warned of potential communication failures due to aging infrastructure and budgetary constraints, telling the FAA in a report that “risk could quickly reach unacceptable levels.”
Last year, a series of disruptions prompted more scrutiny. Outages at a Philadelphia control facility caused the FAA to halt flights at Newark Liberty International Airport. A controller who spoke with CNN anonymously at the time said a single data feed connecting two facilities – similar to an extension cord-like line – had crashed at least twice.
Following the outages, federal investigators questioned whether the FAA had adequately assessed the reliability of telecommunications lines before relocating Newark’s airspace management from New York to Philadelphia. An IG report described a “burnt copper wire” and “failures of both primary and redundant communication infrastructure.”
President Donald Trump’s mega-spending bill passed by Republicans last year included $12.5 billion to start widespread upgrades to the FAA’s infrastructure, a plan Duffy touted at an aviation summit in April.
He said half of the system’s old wires had already been replaced. He referenced the incidents in Newark and blamed outdated wires, stating that since those had been replaced Newark had some of the “most on-time performance.”
“In one year, this administration has done more in replacing old wires than the last administration did in all four of their years,” Duffy told the audience.
Yet the GAO’s September report struck a more cautious note about those plans and criticized the FAA for not having detailed cost estimate and integration plans around its new air traffic control system.
Without doing so, it would “increase the likelihood of FAA repeating its history of cost overruns, delays, and unmet performance targets,” the report found.
The latest mass outage to America’s air traffic control system began as a result of implementing those new upgrades, officials now believe.
Duffy said at a news conference that L3Harris was doing routine maintenance to switch telecommunication lines from copper wires to fiber optics prior to the outage.
After the contractor installed a new router in El Dorado, Arkansas, the device started pinging the FAA networks at a rapid rate on Friday afternoon, according to an FAA statement. A second router in Texas experienced similar issues. The FAA disabled both routers and approximately 60 others as a precaution.
The FAA says that during the outage, 17 of its 22 air route traffic control centers experienced problems.
A telecommunications router suspected of playing a role in the disruption has been sent to a testing facility in Florida, according to a senior administration official.
The FAA and L3Harris are investigating whether the failure was caused by a defective router or an installation or configuration error. The FBI is also involved out of an abundance of caution, the official said.
In a statement, L3Harris said it was supporting the FAA’s investigation and noted the company had already completed more than 70% of the conversion from copper wires to fiber optics.

articles.title_orig: Study estimates magnitude of US data center pollution as climate talks unveil clean AI pledge
articles.title_zh: Study estimates magnitude of US data center pollution as climate talks unveil clean AI pledge
articles.content_orig:
An aerial shows a 49.5 megawatt three-level data center under construction on Oct. 29, 2026 in Vernon, California.
America’s hyperscale data centers together use as much electricity as some entire U.S. states and produce millions of metric tons of carbon dioxide over the course of a year, according to a new study published Monday in Nature Sustainability .
The number of hyperscale data centers, which are larger and more powerful than traditional data centers, and are often used to train and run large-scale AI models , has exploded in recent years. Between 2019 and 2024, the number of data centers around the world doubled from a little over 500 to over 1,100, with more than half located in the United States. That number is only expected to grow: the research firm Synergy estimates that the total capacity of U.S. data centers will double in the next three years, largely driven by the growth of hyperscale data centers .
American voters rallied against data center development in the midterm elections this November, with many citing economic and environmental concerns. In 40 out of 41 local ballot initiatives across the country, citizens voted to limit or prevent data center development. Yet few studies have quantified just how much electricity each hyperscale data center uses, and what fuels generate the electricity, the researchers say.
“Even though there were a lot of [public and scientific] statements about the environmental impact of data centers, when we started this research, we realized that there was basically very little, if none, peer-reviewed data,” says Francesca Dominici, director of the Harvard Data Science Initiative and senior author of the paper.
The study provides one of the first facility-level estimates of the electricity use and carbon dioxide emissions of hyperscale data centers since the rise of AI. The researchers used satellite imagery to build a list of 403 hyperscale data centers across the U.S., and then estimated the annual electricity consumption for each facility between May 2024 and April 2025 under a range of operating scenarios. They then used data from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency to calculate their emissions.
They found that, together, the data centers used between 68 and 99 terawatt-hours (TWh) of electricity—with the upper estimate equivalent to what some states, like Indiana, Michigan, and Tennessee, use in a year. In the lower scenario, the facilities still consumed approximately the annual electricity sold to customers in Wisconsin, roughly 70 TWh, or Minnesota, around 65 TWh.
More than half of the electricity powering the data centers comes from fossil fuels, primarily natural gas and coal. The facilities studied produced a combined estimated 25.7 million metric tons of carbon dioxide—roughly the annual emissions of Denmark.
Half of the electricity use of all the data centers studied was concentrated in just four states: Virginia, Oregon, Ohio, and Iowa, the report found. Virginia has long been known as “data center alley” due to its high number of data centers, but size and power capacity can also impact electricity consumption. The researchers identified 26 hyperscale facilities in Iowa, combined electricity consumption for which was approximately 7.2 TWh, with the average facility having substantially higher estimated electricity demand than the average facility in Virginia, where 142 hyperscale facilities account for approximately 21.4 TWh of annual electricity consumption.
However, the emissions impacts were not always the same. Virginia, Iowa, and Ohio have the most emissions attributable to hyperscale data centers, while Oregon, which is home to more hyperscale data centers than Iowa and Ohio, has significantly fewer emissions due to a cleaner energy grid.
“For the same amount of electricity consumed, the regional electricity mix associated with data centers in Wyoming produces approximately seven times more carbon dioxide than in Oregon,” says Gianluca Guidi, Harvard data scientist and the study’s lead author. “So these environmental impacts are not necessarily inevitable. Geography matters.”
Without clean energy alternatives, U.S. data centers are projected to consume more natural gas than most countries by 2035, according to a report from BloombergNEF.
The electricity demand and carbon emissions are likely even higher than the research shows. The team did not have enough data to assess every single hyperscale data center in the U.S. at the time, and more data centers have emerged since their study concluded in April 2025.
The researchers hope to continue to quantify the environmental impacts of hyperscale data centers to better understand their impact on air pollution, water, and health, adding that, as AI continues to scale, its infrastructure growth must be done sustainably.
“We tend to imagine AI as something that is almost immaterial, but in the end, the infrastructure power is profoundly physical,” says Guidi. “Behind every algorithm, there are enormous buildings, power plants, water resources, and ultimately also communities that live with the consequences.”

articles.title_orig: Splatoon 3 Version 12.0.0 Announced, Here Are The Full Patch Notes
articles.title_zh: Splatoon 3 Version 12.0.0 Announced, Here Are The Full Patch Notes
articles.content_orig:
Nintendo's team-based squid-shooter Splatoon 3 is still going strong, and this week the title is getting updated to Version 12.0.0 .
This major update will come with changes to multiplayer, including weapon adjustments. There are also changes to Anarchy Battle, X Battles and challenges. Additionally, there are changes to the GameChat feature on Switch 2. Nintendo also notes how its next update after this one will focus on multiplayer game balance .
You can get the full rundown in the official patch notes below ( via Nintendo's official support page ):
Subscribe to Nintendo Life on YouTube 855k
Sections marked "on Nintendo Switch 2" apply only to Nintendo Switch 2. All other changes apply to both Nintendo Switch 2 and Nintendo Switch.
Made it possible to participate with a friend in traditional X Battles as a group of two.
Added a feature that allows players to open GameChat and invite friends from their group while playing modes with friends, such as battles or Salmon Run.
This update focuses on making changes to matchmaking and multiplayer balance.
For X Battles, we have added a feature to allow players to play as a pair with a friend. The goal of this feature is to expand the range of ways to play, and we will introduce it on a trial basis starting in Chill Season 2026. After we have introduced it, we will comprehensively analyze how these battles are actually played and how the gameplay situation shifts, including for players who are not playing with a friend. Then we will decide whether to continue providing this feature in future seasons.
For Anarchy Battle (Series), we have changed the matchmaking system such that, in exchange for removing the feature allowing players to continue with the same team, matchmaking will now complete more quickly and with less imbalance of skill level and equipped weapons between players and their opponents.
For Challenges, we have changed how Challenge Power is calculated to make it easier to raise Challenge Power the more wins a player has. With this change, between players who would have ended up with about the same Challenge Power under the previous system, the player who attained the greater number of wins will have the higher final Challenge Power.
For multiplayer balance, we made a variety of changes to main, sub, and special weapons, including changes to the flight distance of Blaster shots.
With most weapons, when a player fires while moving, the player's movement speed is added to the shot's speed to a certain extent, resulting in a more natural trajectory. For Blasters, we have minimized the change in shot flight distance caused by this effect, making it easier to maintain an appropriate distance against an opponent’s Blaster.
Among the special weapons, we have changed the Reefslider because, while there is statistically little impact on victories in matches between extremely skilled players, it has a high impact on matches between less skilled players. The intention behind this change is to alleviate that striking difference. By narrowing the area affected by the explosion we have made it so that players cannot reap the maximum benefit without using it at the precise position. On the other hand, we have extended the invulnerability period to make it harder for opponents who used terrain to survive the explosion to counterattack and easier for the player to make follow-up attacks.
For the Tenta Missiles, we have decreased the vulnerability while firing and expanded the area where it is possible to lock on to opponents. As a result, it will now be easier to use, even in situations where opponents are nearby the player. By decreasing the impact interval, it becomes easier to defeat opponents who are slow to dodge, but the duration for which they must keep dodging is reduced.
We have also added a feature for Nintendo Switch 2 that will make it easier to use GameChat.
The next update will focus on changes to multiplayer balance.
If you haven't already played the game on Switch 2, there's a free upgrade available which includes visual improvements and frame rate optimisations for the platform. In some related news, Splatoon Raiders has also received an eShop demo this week!

articles.title_orig: Asia shares slide on tech weakness ahead of Nvidia earnings
articles.title_zh: Asia shares slide on tech weakness ahead of Nvidia earnings
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
US stocks dropped as investors braced for a momentous week for the artificial intelligence trade, with the Anthropic ( ANTH.PVT ) IPO and Nvidia ( NVDA ) first post-Jensen Huang earnings day on deck.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) fell 1.4%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) declined by roughly 1.9%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) dropped 2.5% after stocks made gains last week despite increased volatility.
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) stock fell 4% during Monday trading as investors mulled what comes next for the chip giant in the wake of its board ousting former CEO Jensen Huang. The board is not considering bringing back Huang, according to a Monday CNBC report. An earlier Financial Times report said Huang and his Silicon Valley allies are discussing a campaign to reinstate him , an idea that President Trump also publicly backed.
On Tuesday, Nvidia will report third quarter results — a consequential earnings report in any typical quarter, but especially significant given Huang's scandal and departure.
That is expected to be followed by Anthropic's IPO on Thursday , which could set the record for the largest public debut of all time and set the tone for OpenAI's ( OPAI.PVT ) eventual IPO. Anthropic is targeting a valuation of around $1.4 trillion.
Oil prices ( CL=F ) dipped , with Brent crude ( BZ=F ) declining to $92 per barrel, as shipments through the Strait of Hormuz continue to recover despite the US ramping up its military presence in the Middle East, as a third US aircraft carrier arrived in the region.
United Airlines ( UAL ) stock fell 3% after the company said it is experiencing a "widespread system outage."
Travelers reported being stuck on flights on the tarmac while they waited for the issue to be resolved.
The outage comes just days after the FAA issued a rare ground stop to all flights due to a "temporary telecommunications outage." On Monday, banking apps and payment services also experienced disruption due to a software bug. Microsoft Outlook also faced a disruption last week.
US stocks sank as Nvidia ( NVDA ) led the semiconductor sector lower following tightened restrictions on advanced chips abroad.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average ( ^DJI ) dropped 1.4%, while the S&P 500 ( ^GSPC ) declined by more than 1.9%. The Nasdaq Composite ( ^IXIC ) sank roughly 2.5%.
This price reflects trading activity during the overnight session on the Blue Ocean ATS, available 8 PM to 4 AM ET, Sunday through Thursday, when regular markets are closed.
Nvidia shares fell roughly 4% after reports said the AI chip giant's board was not considering bringing Jensen Huang back as CEO. Weekend speculation that Silicon Valley executives were pushing for Huang's return was dampened, despite President Trump's public support for the move.
Meanwhile, tighter US restrictions aimed at preventing circumvention of controls on semiconductor access to China weighed on the broader chip sector.
Yahoo Finance's Brian Sozzi reports:
Something pretty remarkable is happening in Silicon Valley right now. One shouldn't be surprised, considering the profit motives of many invested in the AI ecosystem and that what Nvidia ( NVDA ) does lies at the center of it all.
Nvidia founder Jensen Huang resigned as the company's CEO under a cloud of controversy he created, and suddenly some of the biggest names in Silicon Valley are organizing a campaign to bring him back.
Tesla ( TSLA ) and SpaceX ( SPCX ) CEO Elon Musk has signed on to the "Bring Jensen Back" petition. Other prominent executives have joined, including Uber ( UBER ) founder Travis Kalanick — who left Uber unceremoniously after his own string of highly publicized missteps.
Nvidia ( NVDA ) extended declines to session lows on Monday, sinking 4% and dragging the rest of the "Magnificent Seven" group with it.
A snapshot of Yahoo Finance's AlphaSpace data shows t he AI chip giant down 4% while Alphabet ( GOOGL ) shares are down more than 3%. Amazon ( AMZN ) stock is also 3% lower, followed by Meta (META) and Tesla ( TSLA ).
The tech sector retreated, with semiconductor stocks leading the decline after the US tightened restrictions on overseas access to advanced semiconductors.
Reports of bank app outages are causing bank stocks to fall in midday trading. Shares of Bank of America ( BAC ), Citigroup ( C ), Wells Fargo ( WFC ), and JPMorgan Chase ( JPM ) fell by around 2%.
Downdetector.com, which tracks online outages, showed customers' reports of issues spiked across a number of sites, including Chase, US Bank, Truist, and Zelle, which is owned by a privately held company, owned by Bank of America, Truist, Capital Ones, JPMorgan Chase, PNC Bank, US Bank, and Wells Fargo.
"Due to a technical issue, some transactions are taking longer than usual to complete but customers still have access to their accounts and funds. We are working to resolve this as quickly as possible," a JPMorgan spokesperson told Yahoo Finance.
Bank of America ( BAC ) CEO Brian Moynihan gave investors another reason to pay close attention to Anthropic's blockbuster IPO this week.
The Claude maker's massive stock market debut is pushing some smaller companies to delay their own listings until 2027, Moynihan said Monday on Bloomberg TV.
Moynihan said his investment bankers told him over the weekend that companies in more traditional industries, including biotechnology, are postponing offerings to give investors time to digest Anthropic's listing.
"It's just trying to let the market settle in after this major transaction," he added.
Bank of America is estimated to earn around $9 million in underwriting fees from the listing, according to analysis from Evercore ISI.
Nvidia's ( NVDA ) board of directors is reportedly not considering bringing back Jensen Huang as CEO of the AI chip giant.
According to a CNBC report citing a person familiar with the matter, the board is focused on a national security investigation into Huang and is not considering bringing him back.
Nvidia stock fell to session lows after the report.
Huang resigned last Thursday after reports of affairs, including one with a woman reportedly suspected of spying for China.
President Trump on Monday weighed in on the issue, casting doubt on whether the woman was a spy and saying that Huang did not put national security at risk. Trump also supported bringing Huang back to the company.

Intel ( INTC ) stock fell more than 6% Monday morning as the market reacted to news that the company is facing a class action lawsuit from investors, Yahoo Finance's Paige Oamek reports:
In the lawsuit filed on Friday , Intel shareholders claim the technology company misled investors about the impact of a slowdown in PC sales on its revenue. The complaint also claims Intel hid that supply limits blocked the company from meeting data center demand.
When those realities came to light in Intel's third quarter earnings report last month, shares dropped 28.6% the next day, losing around $140 billion of market value in the company's largest single-day decline in more than 50 years.
Vanda Research is telling clients that Anthropic's ( ANTH.PVT ) highly anticipated IPO later this week could attract record buying from everyday investors. But some of that demand may come at the expense of other artificial intelligence stocks.
Vanda Research cautioned clients on Monday that the AI startup's stock market debut could draw money away from tech giants and other data center infrastructure companies that investors have used to gain exposure to the AI boom.
Until now, investors seeking exposure to leading AI developers have largely had to invest indirectly through publicly traded companies backing them or supplying their infrastructure.
